text: Welcome to America's Town Meeting from New York City.
Tonight's subject, flying saucers, fact or illusion.
Our speakers are Major Donald E. Keogh, author of Flying Saucers from Outer Space,
and Jonathan N. Leonard, science editor of Time Magazine and author of Flight Into Space.
For scores of generations, civilized men have recorded astonishing descriptions of atmospheric phenomena
and awesome things hovering in the skies above them.
Mysterious floating objects, flashes and fireballs,
and luminescent manifestations of every description
are recounted in the annals of Western civilization as far back as Roman times.
speculation as to their origin was of course largely conditioned upon the degree of scientific knowledge at the disposal of the observer
generally however they were isolated instances, unrelated and devoid of organized study anywhere
against this historic background, the controversy which has developed in the United States since 1947
over the so-called flying saucer sightings are absolutely without precedent or parallel

An oppressive accumulation of approximately 800 unexplained reports has not only been accorded the widest possible publicity, intriguing the public everywhere and taxing the credulity of many, but has by now enlisted on a national scale the ingenuity of some of our top airmen, scientists, and military experts.
Curiously enough, it is said that more than 18% of these sightings were reported by trained military personnel,
and some 11% were reported by Air Force pilots aloft.
Of all sightings recorded, somewhat less than 15% are reported to be classified as unexplained.
To delve into the mystery of these unexplained phenomena,
the resources of the United States and other nations have mustered at strategic points
scores of special cameras, radar installations, and other detecting devices,
manned by trained personnel.
Meantime, the controversy rages unabated
between those who believe that the so-called flying saucers are facts
and those who dismiss them as an illusion.
Tonight, Town Hall is proud to present two distinguished exponents of each of these viewpoints.

The following year, he finished a training course for naval aviators at Pensacola.
From 1925 to 1927, he was chief of information of the aeronautics branch of the Department of Commerce
and was assigned as manager of the U.S. tour of the Josephine Ford North Pole plane,
which flew around the country with Floyd Bennett and Bert Blanchard.
